expected_evidence: Geological: sediment/boundary-layer geochemistry across European YD-onset sites (~10,950–9,700 cal BCE) re-analyzed for platinum-group-element anomalies, nanodiamonds, magnetic microspherules, and iridium — refutation would show these signals are absent, non-synchronous, or explainable by non-impact processes (e.g., fungal spores, authigenic framboids, wildfire-derived carbon).

Geological/paleoclimate: high-resolution ice-core and lake-sediment records (e.g., Greenland, European varved lakes) showing the YD cooling onset tracks gradual AMOC/meltwater-forcing signatures rather than an abrupt 'impact winter' spike.

Material/archaeological: continuity (rather than abrupt collapse) in Late Upper Paleolithic lithic industries, settlement patterns, and faunal assemblages across Europe spanning the YD boundary, arguing against a sudden catastrophic biomass-burning event.

Paleo-fire proxy data: charcoal/soot/PAH records from European sites tested against the 'continental-scale biomass burning' claim, showing burning levels within normal background variability rather than a synchronous impact-triggered spike.
Astronomical/geological: absence of a dated impact crater or verified extraterrestrial ejecta field matching the ~12.9 ka interval anywhere plausibly linked to Europe.

Genetic: absence of a distinct, impact-attributable population bottleneck signal in European megafauna or human ancient-DNA records specifically dated to 12.9 ka (versus gradual climate-driven decline).

Model-prior: peer-reviewed critical literature (post-2007 rebuttals of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis, e.g., re-analyses failing to replicate spherule/nanodiamond findings) representing the scientific consensus that the impact-winter mechanism is not supported.
response.rationale: This hypothesis is a meta-scientific claim about refutation of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (YDIH) for Europe. Its evidentiary basis is overwhelmingly geological/geochemical (sediment boundary layers, platinum/nanodiamond/spherule analyses, charcoal and paleofire proxies) rather than textual, oral, or iconographic, since no writing systems existed in this pre-Neolithic interval (textual detectability = 0.0, oral_tradition and iconographic ≈ 0.1). The interval [-11000,-10001] falls within the younger-dryas period band, where geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7) detectability are comparatively high — and this is corroborated by the real-world fact that the YDIH debate has in fact been conducted almost entirely through re-examined sediment cores and geochemical datasets across dozens of European and global sites, i.e., the relevant evidence has demonstrably survived and been recovered/published (model-prior, unverified beyond general awareness of this ongoing scientific controversy). Material (archaeological continuity) and genetic (bottleneck) evidence are secondary and only moderately detectable (0.30–0.35). Given that the core evidence type (geological/geochemical stratigraphy) is well-preserved and has already been the primary battleground of this debate in the literature, a modest upward blended adjustment (~0.55) from the raw table averages is warranted, weighting toward the dominant geological/astronomical channels rather than the weak textual/oral/iconographic ones. Absence of confirmatory impact-winter signatures in this window would therefore be meaningful evidence of refutation rather than simply an artifact of poor preservation, though some uncertainty remains because pre-agricultural European sites are unevenly sampled and taphonomic loss of fine sedimentary layers is still possible in places.
